cases.title: Gold 1-hour with VRVP: POC, VAH/VAL, and the short-side liquidity gaps left by the advance
cases.market_context: Gold's 1-hour is around 4595.515, inside a whole consolidation between 4580 and 4640. Price rose fast from a low near 4400 to about 4640 and fell back, leaving a long structureless fast-advance zone, and is now contesting sideways at the highs.
cases.key_observation: Across the visible range the consolidation's POC is near 4615; price above the POC is strong and below it weak. The fast advance added almost no short-side volume (the yellow down value area is absent), which left liquidity gaps above, and the historical 4520–4560 gap is still unfilled.
analysis_steps: Step one: overlay VRVP on gold's 1-hour and distinguish the dark bars (history already traded) from the value area (still being contested), noting that the fast zone above the advance has finished trading.

Step two: lock the visible candles and find the whole consolidation's POC at about 4615. The POC is the balance point between buyers and sellers — above it is strength, below it weakness — and price has retested and bounced off it precisely several times.

Step three: VRVP's drawback is that dragging the chart changes the POC as the visible candles change, so the range has to be pinned; higher timeframes mostly use VRVP and lower ones switch to SVP or the fixed-range profile.
Step four: mark the value area — VAH about 4643, VAL about 4471 — as that consolidation's volume high and low, demonstrating the automatic purple and green resistance and support marks.

Step five: the short-side value area on the advance (the yellow down volume) is almost absent, meaning nobody shorted into the fast rally and the shorts became fuel for the longs; price rose fast and the long-side volume was not high either.

Step six: the middle of that fast advance had no structural support, leaving a major liquidity gap — the whole segment is an FVG. The historical gap around 4520 to 4560 (January 8 to 12) is still unfilled; VP infers future support and resistance from past behaviour.
Step seven: combined with order blocks, the 1233 run inside that gap zone yields a bullish order block for a pullback long, with below 4500 as the reference for a structural break.
cases.lessons: VRVP's visible range has to be pinned to keep the POC stable; above the POC is strength and below it weakness. A fast advance with no short-side volume leaves a liquidity gap (an FVG) above, and combining VAH/VAL with order blocks locates the unfilled gaps and the support and resistance. VP is passive by nature and has to be used alongside the trend and the moving averages.

cases.title: Gold 6-hour: the crash filling every gap, with each wick point matching one
cases.market_context: Gold rose from around 4258 to about 4680 and fell back into the 4300s. The earlier fast advance left several liquidity gaps (LVNs) below. Price is now about 4595, oscillating near the EMA20 (about 4584) and the EMA60 (about 4503).
cases.key_observation: On the 6-hour, the decline that night filled every liquidity gap below one by one, and each wick point matches a prior gap exactly. Market makers took out all the buy-side liquidity above first, then bounced.
analysis_steps: Step one: decide which timeframe key levels like 4500 belong to. Start with the 6-hour, and confirm every one of them corresponds there.

Step two: VRVP's drawback is that the POC changes substantially when the chart is dragged or the timeframe switched, so hide POC, VAH and VAL and use the volume distribution only for liquidity, or the trade comes out skewed.
Step three: on the 6-hour, mark the several enormous liquidity gap zones price passed through, block by block.
Step four: after the gaps were taken out price rose, retail contested at the highs (the green box around 4520–4560), and price then retested each gap below in turn.

Step five: explain why the decline that night was inevitable — a rally leaving enormous gaps must fill them. Market makers took out all the buy-side liquidity, price was driven hard back into the 4300s, every gap was filled, and every wick point matched a gap.
Step six: conclude that once the gaps were filled and the buy-side liquidity exhausted, price bounced naturally and shorting had no point; map the same logic back to the 1-hour.
cases.lessons: A liquidity gap (LVN) left by a fast advance is very likely to be filled, and the wick points usually match the gaps one for one; market makers sweep the buy-side liquidity clean before bouncing. When using VRVP, hide POC, VAH and VAL so a POC that moves on a timeframe switch does not mislead the read.

cases.title: Gold 1-hour downtrend and the call for a market-maker break-the-low-and-turn
cases.market_context: Gold's 1-hour is still in a downtrend, with the EMA60 broken and a bearish cross of the fast through the slow about to spread lower. The 4600 POC is a band of dense prior long volume that price has repeatedly failed to clear. Price is about 4595; the screenshot is mid-January 2026.
cases.key_observation: Reading VRVP's liquidity distribution, the instructor says the 4600 POC will not be cleared, that a huge liquidity gap sits across 4500 to 4560, and that retail long orders are dense around 4480 (the blue bid bars are thicker than the yellow) — which makes it hard for market makers to genuinely break price down and let retail get filled buying the dip.
analysis_steps: Step one: read the liquidity distribution with VRVP, identifying the green box at about 4520–4560 as a bullish order block, already retested.
Step two: on the 1-hour, judge the trend — still down, with the same timeframe's EMA60 broken and the fast line crossing the slow into a bearish cross about to spread lower.
Step three: review Friday's liquidity — the 5-minute and 15-minute liquidity is at 4600, and the 4600 POC is the dense prior retail long band that price never clears.
Step four: anticipate the market maker's trick — around the 4475 VAL they may sweep liquidity once more, manufacturing the appearance of a decline to induce retail to turn bearish.
Step five: from the VP view the real liquidity gap is the large 4500–4560 band, with 4560–4520 as very strong 4-hour and 12-hour moving-average support and a high probability of a bounce.

Step six: the blue bid bars near 4480 are thicker than the yellow, which proves retail long orders are dense there; market makers will not let retail get filled buying the dip easily, which implies price will struggle to genuinely reach that zone.
Step seven: on the 12-hour, the fundamental support is 4412, the 12-hour limit; breaking through 4412 is very unlikely, since it would destroy the bull-market logic.
Step eight: on balance, price very probably tests here once more, consolidates, then plays a break-the-low-and-turn back up.

cases.title: Gold's earlier $230/$390 crashes reviewed: institutions hunting short stops and filling the imbalances
cases.market_context: Gold has previously crashed $230 at speed, leaving a mass of order blocks and imbalance gaps on the way. The instructor reviews the December 2025 4-hour advance gaps as the example, analysing how institutions trade the fills.
cases.key_observation: The fast $230 decline killed nearly every long in the market, so market makers have no interest in pressing lower; institutions have to BUY to take out retail short stops, filling the imbalance gaps left on the way and even reversing to a new high.
analysis_steps: Step one: in a fast decline institutions only need to take out retail stops (the taker/maker logic) rather than genuinely buy; retail shorts all get eaten.

Step two: a mass of resting orders sits in the imbalance zone (the FVG, which is not a buy zone), and institutions bring price back into those zones to hunt that liquidity — which is why the gaps must be filled.
Step three: use VRVP to see the many order-block zones and liquidity gaps this fast decline produced; price falling to here only gets pressed back up, with 4360 as the lowest fill target.
Step four: a 4-hour bullish divergence below provides multiple validation, which is why price then bounced — direction read from liquidity.

Step five: think in reverse — after a $230 crash the longs are essentially all dead, so pressing lower is pointless and makes no money; institutions must use buys to kill the retail shorts and fill the gaps.
Step six: switch to the 4-hour and set VRVP's row count to 250 so the gaps render finely, then review the mass of gaps December 2025's advance left, demonstrating that gaps do get filled in the end.
cases.lessons: The imbalance gaps and order blocks left by a fast crash are very likely to be filled; institutions lead price by hunting short stops and filling gaps. Think against human instinct: once the longs are wiped out, institutions can only continue by buying, and the gap gets filled.

cases.title: Top gold traders skip the HVN chop entirely and commit only on the retest after VAH liquidity is swept
cases.market_context: After a fast advance, gold's 1-hour has chopped sideways between roughly 4580 and 4640 for about fifteen candles. VRVP on the left shows 4440–4560 as the largest volume node (the HVN peak); price is about 4595, oscillating above the green support rectangle at 4520–4560.
cases.key_observation: VRVP shows retail contesting densely inside the HVN high-volume node (about 4480–4560). That whole band is unlikely to break immediately, holds no institutional orders and carries no trading value; the real key level is the retest after the VAH liquidity at about 4463 has been swept.
analysis_steps: Step 1: pull up the VRVP volume profile and identify 4440–4560 on the left as the largest volume node (the HVN peak) — the asset's balanced value area.
Step 2: retail chops and contests continuously inside that HVN band, and the market is unlikely to break through the high-volume range immediately.
Step 3: the longer the volume bar at a price, the less likely an institutional order sits there; institutions act only at the two ends of the range and will not fight retail in the middle.
Step 4: conclude that top higher-timeframe traders skip the entire HVN chop, because it has no trading value.
Step 5: mark the VAH at about 4463 and wait for the liquidity there to be swept.
Step 6: once the liquidity is swept and price retests, commit size at the retest with the stop only a little below; combined with other indicators this can carry to above 4700.

Step 7: add that the European session is the worst of it for retail order placement — the high-volume nodes mostly form in the afternoon overlap of the Asian and European sessions — so find the low-volume node (LVN) rather than placing orders inside the HVN.
cases.outcome: Given as an illustration: top traders skip the whole HVN, wait for the VAH liquidity to be swept, and commit on the retest, potentially carrying straight to above 4700. It is a teaching demonstration, not a live trade record.
cases.lessons: Skilled traders skip the HVN chop rather than fight retail there, and enter with size only on the retest after liquidity at a key level such as VAH has been swept. The longer the volume bar, the less likely an institutional order sits there — find the LVN, not the HVN; the European session is retail's worst zone and carries no trading value.
